records.text: Visual BERT was one of the first successful attempts to handle pictures with transformers.
Visual BERT was designed primarily for image captioning.
The idea of Visual BERT was to feed both text tokens and object tokens into a single Transformer.
Object tokens are vectors representing specific objects found on the picture.

To obtain object tokens, one must first solve object detection, extract the bounding boxes of objects, embed them into vectors (e.g., via a CNN), and feed the resulting sequence alongside the caption.
The Transformer in Visual BERT learns to attend across modalities.
For instance, words in the caption attend to the corresponding image regions.
The key insight is that a Transformer treats any sequence of vectors uniformly, regardless of whether those vectors came from text or images.
The Visual BERT approach paved the way for applying Transformers to vision directly.
The Vision Transformer (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) applies a standard Transformer encoder to images without any text input.
In ViT, an image $x \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$ is split into $N = HW / P^2$ patches of size $P \times P$.
Each patch is flattened and projected linearly into an embedding vector, forming a sequence $x_p \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times P^2 C}$.
The sequence is fed into a Transformer encoder exactly like BERT.
The pretraining objective of ViT is masked patch modeling: half of the input embeddings are replaced by a learnable `[mask]` embedding, and the model must reconstruct the original patch content.
Positional encodings are added to preserve spatial information in ViT.
The original ViT uses the same 1D positional encodings as the text Transformer.
The authors of ViT experimented with 2D encodings but found no improvement.
Treating the grid as a simple sequence works perfectly well in ViT.
ViT revolutionized computer vision because the Transformer extracts richer, more semantically meaningful features than convolutional networks.
In many applications, one can simply replace a CNN backbone with ViT and get better results.
Hundreds of papers after 2020 exploited the fact that ViT can replace CNN backbones with better results.
Every Transformer has an attention matrix of size $L \times L$ where $L$ is the input length.
For ViT, $L$ equals the number of patches, so the complexity grows quadratically with the number of patches.
This quadratic complexity forbids using very small patches (to capture fine details) because even a million-pixel input would require an infeasible $10^{12}$ attention weights.
Therefore, ViT must use relatively large patches, which means small details (like a distant cat sitting entirely inside one patch) may be lost.
There is no perfect patch size: too large loses detail, too small is computationally impossible.
The Swin Transformer (Liu et al., 2021) addresses the quadratic complexity while preserving the ability to capture fine details and global context.
The name Swin stands for Shifted windows.
In Swin Transformer hierarchical processing, instead of feeding the entire fine grid to a self-attention layer, the image is broken into smaller windows.
Within each window, self-attention complexity is only quadratic in the window size, not the whole image.
Swin Transformer starts with small windows on a fine grid to process locally.
Swin Transformer merges features from neighbouring windows to process at a coarser scale.
Swin Transformer repeats these steps, finally processing the whole image at a coarse level.
At every scale in Swin Transformer, transformer layers only ever see a fixed, small number of tokens (e.g., $4 \times 4 = 16$).
This reduces the overall complexity from $O(N^2)$ to roughly linear in the number of patches.
The downside of strict window partitioning is that features cannot communicate across windows, losing global context.
Global context is essential: a small white blob on a highway is probably a car, but the same blob on water is a boat; you cannot classify it without seeing the surroundings.
The Swin Transformer solves the communication problem with window shifting: between consecutive self-attention layers, the grid of windows is shifted by half a window size.
A feature that belonged to one window in layer $\ell$ will belong to a different, overlapping window in layer $\ell+1$.
Over several layers in Swin Transformer, the receptive field expands, allowing information to propagate across the whole image.
Shifting creates incomplete windows at the image edges.
The original implementation of Swin Transformer wraps the image around a torus, grouping leftover parts together.
The border-handling code of Swin Transformer becomes extremely convoluted, especially in 3D versions.
Swin Transformer v2 (Liu et al., 2022) scaled the architecture to 3 billion parameters and input resolutions up to $1536 \times 1536$, achieving state-of-the-art results across many vision tasks.
Swin and ViT are the two dominant backbones for modern computer vision.
A backbone is the part of the network that performs feature extraction; task-specific heads (classification, detection, segmentation) can later be attached on top.
Object detection is the task of localising and classifying multiple objects in an image.
For each object of interest in object detection, we must predict a bounding box defined by four numbers $(x, y, w, h)$: the coordinates of one corner and the width and height.
For each object of interest, we must also predict a class label, given as a probability distribution over known classes.
Neural networks require a fixed output size, but an image can contain a varying number of objects.
The standard solution is to fix a maximum number of objects $K$ that the network will output.
Each of the $K$ slots predicts a confidence score (probability that a real object exists in that slot), a class distribution (only meaningful if an object is present), and a bounding box.
During training, most slots will be empty, so their confidence is driven to zero.
The ground truth in object detection consists of a set of objects (class + box).
The network's output slots do not have a predefined order (e.g., there is no reason slot 1 must correspond to the cat and slot 2 to the dog).
Therefore, training requires solving an assignment problem: find the optimal one-to-one matching between ground-truth objects and predicted slots that minimises a total cost.
The cost for matching a ground-truth object $y_i = (c_i, b_i)$ to a prediction $\hat{y}_{\sigma(i)}$ combines classification error and bounding box error.
The matching is typically done with the Hungarian algorithm, which yields a bipartite matching.
Once the optimal matching $\sigma^*$ is found, the actual training loss is computed only for the matched pairs.
Confidence loss: for matched real objects the confidence should be 1; for unmatched slots it should be 0. This loss is often a binary cross-entropy (log-confidence).
Classification loss: for matched objects, a cross-entropy between the predicted class distribution and the true class.
Bounding box regression loss: for matched objects, the predicted box $(x, y, w, h)$ must match the ground-truth box.

The overall loss can be written as: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Hungarian}}(y, \hat{y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \Big[ -\log \hat{p}_{\sigma^*(i)}(c_i) + \mathbb{1}_{\{c_i \neq \emptyset\}} \, \mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}(b_i, \hat{b}_{\sigma^*(i)}) \Big]$, where empty objects get a smaller weight in practice.
A simple coordinate-wise $L_1$ or $L_2$ loss for bounding boxes has a problem: the same numerical error in $x$ or $w$ matters much more for small objects than for large ones.
A small shift may cause zero overlap for a tiny box, while it barely affects a large box.
The standard metric for bounding box evaluation is IoU, defined as $\text{IoU}(B_1, B_2) = \frac{\text{area}(B_1 \cap B_2)}{\text{area}(B_1 \cup B_2)}$.
IoU naturally scales between 0 and 1, and it is differentiable provided the boxes overlap.
However, when boxes do not overlap, IoU is exactly 0 and its gradient is zero, giving the network no signal about the direction to move.

This led to extensions such as Generalized IoU (GIoU), which considers the smallest enclosing box and penalises distance between non-overlapping boxes, providing a meaningful gradient even when IoU is zero.

During training, when computing the assignment, a predicted box is only allowed to match a ground-truth box if its IoU exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.5). Otherwise it is treated as background (confidence driven to 0).
This prevents far-away boxes from being incorrectly assigned to an object.
At test time, the network often produces many overlapping high-confidence boxes around the same object.
To obtain a clean output, non-maximum suppression is applied: boxes with the highest confidence are kept, and lower-confidence boxes with high IoU overlap are suppressed.
NMS is a non-differentiable handcrafted step used only at inference; during training, the matching already handles duplicates implicitly.
The first successful deep-learning detector was R-CNN (Girshick et al., 2014).

R-CNN follows a two-stage approach. The first stage is region proposal: an external algorithm, selective search, generates around 2000 candidate bounding boxes that may contain objects (regardless of class).
The second stage is per-region classification: each candidate box is warped to a fixed square size (e.g., 224x224) and passed through a CNN pretrained on ImageNet to extract features.
Those features are then classified by a separate SVM to determine the object class.
An additional linear regressor refines the bounding box coordinates.
R-CNN had multi-stage training: CNN fine-tuning, SVM training, and bounding-box regressor training were separate stages.
R-CNN was extremely slow: each of the 2000 regions required a full CNN forward pass, taking about 47 seconds per image on a GPU.
The external region proposal in R-CNN is a bottleneck and not trainable.
Fast R-CNN (Girshick, 2014) kept the two-stage philosophy but made two crucial improvements.
In Fast R-CNN, the entire image is passed through a convolutional backbone only once, producing a feature map.
For each region proposal, the corresponding part of the feature map is cropped via RoI (Region of Interest) projection.

Since the feature map retains some spatial geometry, each proposal maps to a fixed-size feature block through RoI pooling: the block is divided into a fixed grid (e.g., 2x2) and max-pooled, yielding a constant-size representation regardless of the original proposal size.
In Fast R-CNN, a single small detection head (classifier + bounding-box regressor) processes each pooled feature.
This made Fast R-CNN two orders of magnitude faster than R-CNN with no loss in accuracy.
However, in Fast R-CNN, region proposals still came from an external, non-learned algorithm (selective search).
Faster R-CNN (Ren et al., 2015) removed the last non-learned component.
Faster R-CNN introduced a Region Proposal Network (RPN) that operates on the same feature map.

The RPN slides a small network over the feature map and, at each location, evaluates a set of predefined anchor boxes (various scales and aspect ratios) and outputs an objectness score and a box refinement.
The top-scoring proposals from the RPN are then fed to the same RoI pooling and detection head as in Fast R-CNN.
Faster R-CNN became the standard detector for several years: it was completely end-to-end trainable and could be used with any convolutional backbone (VGG, ResNet, EfficientNet, etc.).

All subsequent improvements in backbones automatically translated into better detection in Faster R-CNN, a hallmark of meta-architectures: the detection head and proposal mechanism are fixed, and only the feature extractor is swapped.
Faster R-CNN is a two-stage detector: it first proposes regions, then classifies and refines them.
In contrast, one-stage detectors skip the proposal step and directly predict class and box for a dense set of candidate locations in a single pass.
The most famous one-stage family is YOLO (You Only Look Once; Redmon et al., 2016).
In YOLO, the image is divided into an $S \times S$ grid.
Each grid cell in YOLO predicts $B$ bounding boxes (each with $x, y, w, h$ and a confidence score) and class probabilities for the cell (conditioned on an object being present).
The YOLO detector's output is a tensor of shape $S \times S \times (5B + C)$.
YOLO is trained end-to-end with a single, unified loss.
YOLO trades a slight drop in accuracy for dramatically faster inference.
YOLO is suitable for real-time applications.
Subsequent versions of YOLO (YOLOv2, YOLOv3, etc.) refined the architecture.
The refinements include better backbones, anchor boxes, multi-scale training, and hierarchical softmax for large class sets.
Each refinement added a few percentage points to the mean Average Precision.
Across all object detectors, detecting small objects is the hardest challenge.
Detecting a large object that occupies a quarter of the image is easy.
A tiny distant object may only cover a few pixels.
In a CNN backbone, as we go deeper, we lose spatial resolution and the feature map becomes coarser.
A small object will eventually fit entirely inside one feature vector, and its identity is lost.
Stopping the backbone early to keep a fine grid results in features that are not semantically rich enough.
Processing all fine-grid locations is computationally prohibitive.
Multi-scale detection is the solution to the small-object problem.
In multi-scale detection, detection heads are attached at multiple stages of the backbone, where the grid is fine for small objects and coarse for large objects.
Fine-scale features lack global context.
Global context is often crucial for recognising small objects.
A few pixels of an animal can be a car or a boat depending on surroundings.
Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) addresses the lack of global context in fine-scale features by adding top-down pathways.
In FPN, high-level, semantically strong features from deeper, coarser layers are upsampled and merged with fine-scale features via lateral connections.
The resulting feature pyramid gives every scale access to rich semantic information.
FPN was a very influential idea.
FPN remains a staple in modern detectors.
Architectures like EfficientDet used neural architecture search to automatically design the optimal FPN connections.
Classical detectors rely on hand-crafted components: anchor boxes, region proposals, and non-maximum suppression.
The components of classical detectors are tuned manually.
Non-maximum suppression (NMS) is a non-differentiable post-processing step.
The transformer philosophy suggests treating detection as a set prediction problem, where the transformer directly outputs the set of objects with no anchors and no NMS.
DETR (Carion et al., 2020) is the first detector to fully embrace the set prediction approach.
The DETR architecture is an encoder-decoder Transformer applied to image features.
In DETR, a standard CNN backbone (e.g., ResNet) extracts a feature map from the image.
The feature map is flattened into a sequence of tokens, and positional encodings are added.
The Transformer encoder processes the token sequence, mixing global context.
The encoder does not perform detection itself.
The encoder refines the features to be suitable for detection.
The Transformer decoder takes a fixed set of object queries.
Object queries are learned positional embeddings independent of the image.
Each object query is a slot for one potential object.
The decoder uses cross-attention to gather information from the encoder output.
The decoder uses self-attention to coordinate among queries so they do not duplicate the same object.
The output of each query passes through a feed-forward detection head that predicts the class and bounding box, or 'no object'.
The number of objects detected equals the number of object queries, typically $N=100$.
Because the queries exchange information through self-attention, they specialise, with different queries learning to focus on different spatial locations and object sizes.
DETR does not need non-maximum suppression because multiple queries will not all converge to the same object.
DETR uses a set prediction loss that involves bipartite matching.
DETR uses the Hungarian algorithm to find the optimal permutation between its N predictions and the ground truth objects padded with $\emptyset$ to size N.

The matching cost minimized by the Hungarian algorithm is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{match}}(y_i, \hat{y}_{\sigma(i)}) = -\mathbb{1}_{\{c_i \neq \emptyset\}} \hat{p}_{\sigma(i)}(c_i) + \mathbb{1}_{\{c_i \neq \emptyset\}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}(b_i, \hat{b}_{\sigma(i)})$.
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}$ combines $L_1$ loss and GIoU loss.
After matching, the training loss sums negative log-likelihood for the matched classes and the bounding box loss for non-empty objects.
Empty objects are down-weighted in the training loss.
The original DETR processes features at a single scale, which makes it weak on small objects.
Visualizing decoder attention in DETR shows that attention weights concentrate on object boundaries.
This boundary attention is sufficient for classification and box refinement once objects have been separated by the encoder.
The quadratic complexity of standard self-attention prevents simply running DETR on a fine multi-scale grid.
Deformable DETR (Zhu et al., 2021) solves the scale problem by using deformable attention.
In deformable attention, each attention head attends to only a small, learned set of sampling points around a reference point.
This reduces the complexity from $O(L^2)$ to $O(L K)$ where $K \ll L$ is the number of sampled points.
With this efficiency, Deformable DETR can process multi-scale feature maps from different backbone layers without blowing up computation.
Deformable DETR detects small objects much better while keeping the end-to-end, NMS-free philosophy.
One weakness of DETR is that object queries (abstract vectors) learn to specialise very slowly.
A sequence of works re-interpreted DETR's object queries as anchor boxes.
These works introduced mechanisms to speed up training and improve detection.
In DAB-DETR (Dynamic Anchor Box DETR; Liu et al., 2022), each query is an explicit 4-tuple $(x, y, w, h)$ anchor box that is refined layer by layer in the decoder.
The width and height modulate cross-attention to localise attention around the box.
This gives clear semantics and faster convergence.
DN-DETR (Denoising DETR; Li et al., 2022) tackles the instability of Hungarian matching during early training.
DN-DETR adds a denoising objective where extra queries are fed noisy versions of ground truth boxes and the network must reconstruct the clean boxes.
This denoising objective provides a 'good anchor' signal that stabilises offset prediction and keeps queries close to their targets.
DINO (DETR with Improved DeNoising anchor boxes; Zhang et al., 2022) further improves DN-DETR.
DINO introduces negative examples (bad anchors that should be rejected).
DINO uses a mixed query selection strategy where positional queries are initialised from encoder proposals and content queries remain learned.
DINO uses a look-ahead training scheme with two-step gradient blocking that improves box quality.
DINO achieves state-of-the-art results with much faster training.
These detectors (DAB-DETR, DN-DETR, DINO) share the core DETR idea.
The core DETR idea is that object queries are slots filled with content by the transformer decoder attending to the image.
This makes the entire detection pipeline a learned set-prediction machine that eliminates hand-crafted anchors and NMS while offering excellent performance.
